title: POC Weekly - Caching & KV hit-rate sync
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on prefix/KV caching results, hit-rate improvements, prompt reuse strategy, and tuning next steps. We reviewed metrics from last week's benchmark, discussed normalization and TTL strategies, and agreed on experiments to raise hot-prefix hit rates and reduce tokens per request. Action items assigned for a short benchmarking pass and a dashboard update.
action_items: Owner: Leon Chen | Item: Run 8-hour hot-prefix focused benchmark with client-side prompt normalization enabled | Due: 2025-03-20
Owner: Priya Nair | Item: Provide sample of top 200 user prompts and groupings for prefix mapping | Due: 2025-03-19
Owner: Sofia Ramos | Item: Add cache efficiency panel to shared dashboard (KV hit-rate by prefix + tokens saved) | Due: 2025-03-21
Owner: Maya Patel | Item: Share updated pricing impact spreadsheet with projected token savings from improved hit rates | Due: 2025-03-20
next_steps: Leon to run targeted benchmark with normalization + high TTL to measure delta in hit rate
Customer to share prompt corpus for prefix grouping and hot key identification
Redwood to push a config to increase default prefix TTL from 1h to 6h for hot prefixes during the pilot
Schedule follow-up sync next Tuesday to review benchmark and dashboard (30 min)
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-03-18 14:00 PDT | Duration: 40m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Leon (Redwood SE), Sofia (Redwood SRE); Carlos (DataWave CTO), Priya (ML Eng), Evan (SRE)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining the weekly POC sync. Quick agenda — hit-rate review on KV/prefix cache, prompt reuse patterns, tuning we tried last week, and next steps. Carlos, anything to add?

[00:22] Carlos: No, that covers it. We're mainly seeing variability in hit-rate across different user cohorts and want to understand tradeoffs if we increase TTLs or normalize prompts.

[00:35] Leon: Great, I'll walk through the dashboard numbers first. Quick note, the dashboard link I shared is the live one — folks might see small sampling delay. Last 24h overall KV hit-rate is at ~46% for the pilot group, prefix cache hit-rate is 38% — so tokens saved per request improved by roughly 12% compared to baseline.

[01:10] Priya: That aligns w/ what we saw internally. The problem is the long tail — some prefixes are 70% hit, others are near 0. A lot of user prompts are slightly different because of personalization tokens and timestamps.

[01:28] Leon: Exactly. That's why we tested client-side prompt normalization last run — lowercasing, stripping timestamps, and templating user-specific fields. The run with normalization bumped prefix hit-rate from 38% to 54% in the controlled subset.

[01:50] Evan: Wait, the normalization run — was that on Hosted or Dedicated? I thought you said Dedicated cached state is separate.

[01:58] Sofia: Good question. That experiment was on the Dedicated pilot pool (the pilot is on dedicated capacity). Cache is per-pool, so normalization improvements should be stable for that pool. We also tried a small TTL bump to 3h for the top 50 prefixes — that showed an additional ~6% improvement but introduced some memory pressure on the nodes.

[02:25] Carlos: Memory pressure — can you quantify? We can't afford instability.

[02:30] Sofia: On the cluster we saw cache footprint increase by about 12% when top prefixes had 3h TTL. With current node sizing it's okay, but if we globally increase TTL we could exceed safe margins during peak. We recommend targeted TTL for hot prefixes only.

[02:52] Maya: That's consistent with Redwood's suggested approach — target hot prefixes, enable client normalization, and run a hot-prefix detection job that updates which prefixes get elevated TTL.

[03:05] Priya: How are you detecting hot prefixes now? Is it server side only?

[03:10] Leon: The detector is server-side: we aggregate prefix request counts in a rolling 6-hour window and mark the top X% as hot. For the pilot we used top 5% threshold. We can also expose that list via an API if you want to do client-side tagging.

[03:30] Priya: Expose via API would be ideal — then we can pre-tag known heavy flows and avoid cold misses during spikes.

[03:36] Leon: We can do that. One caveat: the detector uses normalized prefixes, so if you do client normalization differently we could get mismatch. We should align normalization rules.

[03:50] Evan: Are there any regressions in output quality when normalization is applied? Some prompts rely on capitalization or date tokens.

[03:58] Priya: We did a small qualitative check — outputs were functionally equivalent; only small formatting differences. But we'd like a small evaluation set to be sure.

[04:12] Leon: Good call. We'll run the normalized vs raw A/B on the evaluation set — check for semantic/regression issues.

[04:20] Maya: Let's talk numbers from the latest benchmark. Leon, you sent last night's CSV; can you summarize the key deltas?

[04:28] Leon: Sure. Baseline avg tokens/request: 180. With prefix caching baseline tokens dropped to avg 158 (12% cost reduction). With client normalization and targeted TTL increase, avg tokens/request dropped to 137 (24% total improvement vs baseline). End-to-end latency improved marginally — about 5–10% for cached requests, but overall p95 didn't move much because uncached tails still dominate.

[05:00] Carlos: So caching helps cost — but latency benefit is limited unless we get the tail to hit more.

[05:06] Leon: Correct. The tail is the problem. That's why prompt reuse — making prompts more similar — is high ROI.

[05:12] Priya: We're worried about personalization leakage if we normalize too aggressively — e.g., removing user IDs is fine, but we need to keep context.

[05:20] Sofia: Normalization should be a templating step: replace PII tokens with placeholders rather than drop context. That preserves structure for the model while improving cacheability.

[05:33] Evan: Could you share the normalization library or rules?

[05:36] Maya: We'll share the suggested normalization guidelines and a sample client lib. Link in chat after the call.

[05:44] Priya: About eviction — what policy does Redwood use? LRU? Weighted?

[05:48] Leon: We use a hybrid LRU with weight by token-size; prefixes with high request frequency get sticky TTL bump via the hot-prefix detector. That lets us avoid evicting high-throughput prefixes prematurely.

[06:06] Carlos: Any observed regressions from sticky TTL? For example, stale prefixes responding with outdated instructions?

[06:12] Sofia: We haven't seen semantic staleness in the pilot; most prefixes are stable templates. If you have dynamic system prompts, we recommend version-tagging prefixes (e.g., include model-version or policy-version in prefix key) so cache invalidation happens with version change.

[06:30] Priya: Good point — we do update policy occasionally; we'll version our system prompt.

[06:36] Leon: I'll note that as an action.

[06:40] Maya: Let's surface one of the problematic cohorts — the onboarding flow. Priya, you mentioned onboarding inputs vary a lot?

[06:48] Priya: Yes, new users write freeform bios that include emojis, special chars, timestamps. That kills prefix similarity. We're proposing a lightweight client sanitizer that canonicalizes emojis and removes created_at timestamps.

[07:03] Carlos: What's the expected hit-rate improvement from that single change?

[07:06] Leon: In our internal run, canonicalizing emojis and stripping timestamps increased hit-rate for onboarding flows from 22% to 61% in the test set — huge win.

[07:18] Evan: Wow. Memory impact?

[07:21] Sofia: Not significant at the prefix level; more requests become shared so cache efficiency improves, which can reduce total footprint. However if many different users have similar normalized prefixes we may see hot keys get larger, but that's fine.

[07:35] Maya: On the instrumentation side — we added a new panel that shows KV hit-rate by prefix and tokens-saved. Sofia, can you recap what's in the dashboard?

[07:44] Sofia: Sure — panel A: overall KV/prefix hit-rate over time; panel B: top 50 prefixes by request count and hit-rate; panel C: tokens saved per prefix; panel D: memory utilization per node. The dashboard is shared in the pilot workspace (link in meeting notes).

[08:02] Priya: We looked at top 10 prefixes and saw most savings concentrated — classic long-tail. Makes sense.

[08:08] Leon: For next experiment we propose: 1) client-side normalization enabled for a subset of flows, 2) detector-based hot-prefix TTL bump to 6h for top 2% prefixes, and 3) run 8-hour continuous benchmark during business hours to capture peak patterns.

[08:26] Carlos: Sounds reasonable. What about rollback — if memory spikes, how do you handle?

[08:31] Sofia: We have an automated throttle: if node memory crosses 80% we revert TTL bump for the lowest ranked hot prefixes and emit alerts. We can make that threshold more conservative for you.

[08:45] Maya: Also, from a cost perspective, Leon will share the updated token-savings vs projected spend sheet so you can see dollar impact.

[08:54] Priya: Please include both hosted and dedicated projections — we may move some traffic to hosted for cost experiments.

[09:02] Leon: Will do. One more note — we found a small bug in prefix canonicalization where punctuation normalization removed meaningful separators in a few templates; Leon: that's me — I'll patch and re-run.

[09:18] Priya: Good catch.

[09:20] Carlos: Are there any security / compliance concerns with caching? We need to confirm no PII is stored unencrypted and that audit logs capture cache hits.

[09:30] Sofia: Cache keys do not store raw PII — normalized keys replace PII with placeholders. Cached values are encrypted at rest and we log cache ops; we can provide audit logs for the pilot. We'll share SOC2 artifact links.

[09:48] Priya: Please share the audit log format so our compliance team can review.

[09:52] Maya: Action: Maya to share security doc + audit log sample.

[10:00] [10:00] Wrap-up and recap.

[10:03] Maya: Recap — Leon runs benchmark with normalization and 6h TTL for top prefixes; Priya shares prompt corpus; Sofia adds dashboard panel; Maya shares pricing and security docs. Schedule follow-up next Tuesday. Thanks everyone.

[10:20] End of recording.
